Learning New Songs; Series 2 BUILD IT INTO YOUR MEMORY From “I Recognise It” to “I Can Perform It” One of the biggest mistakes learners make is listening to a song repeatedly and assuming they have learned it. The real test comes when the recording stops. Can you continue? Use the Memory Test Stop the recording. Sing or play the section from memory. Identify what you missed. Go back to that specific phrase. Practise it again. Test yourself once more. This turns passive listening into active learning. Break the Song Into Sections Instead of treating a song as one large task, divide it into manageable parts: Intro → Verse → Chorus → Vamp → Bridge → Final Chorus → Ending You might work on the verse today, the chorus tomorrow and the bridge later. The exact schedule can change depending on the difficulty of the song. The principle remains: L e a r n → R e c a l l → C o n n e c t → T e s t For Singers Don’t learn only the lyrics. Listen for: Where each phrase begins and ends Breathing points Intervals and difficult notes Changes in melody Pronunciation Dynamics Runs and embellishments A useful exercise is to sing the melody on “la” before adding the lyrics. This helps expose pitch and rhythm problems that words can sometimes hide. For Instrumentalists Challenge yourself before immediately searching for a tutorial. If you hear a melody, try to find it. If you hear the bass movement, try to identify it. If you hear a chord change, try to work out what is happening. You can then use notation, chord charts or tutorials to confirm your work. This develops both technical ability and musical independence. For Choirs Knowing your individual part is only the beginning. Your part makes no true meaning if you don’t understand the relational structure that brings other individual parts together.” Once each section is reasonably secure, begin combining the parts. Listen beyond your own voice. Hear how your part fits with the soprano, alto, tenor, bass, instrumental accompaniment and overall arrangement. A strong choir is not simply a group of people who know their individual parts. It is an ensemble that understands how those parts work together. In my experience as a music director and choir trainer, rehearsals become much more productive when singers arrive already familiar with their sections. Rehearsal can then focus on blend, balance, dynamics, interpretation and musical communication rather than learning every note from scratch. PRACTICE PLAN — 60 MINUTES Listen to the complete song – 10 minutes Work on the most difficult section – 20minutes Perform that section from memory – 10 minutes Connect it to the previous or next section – 10 minutes Record yourself and identify one area to improve – 10minutes Today’s goal: Perform at least one complete section confidently without the recording. “A recording can guide you, a score can instruct you, and a teacher can correct you—but true musicianship develops when your own ears begin to guide you.”— Victor Adenola But there is one final stage. Knowing every part of a song does not automatically make you ready to perform it.
